```{r}
getwd()
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/scout.db")
postings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "scout_postings") |> tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

jobs = postings |>
  dplyr::select(company, title, location_state, remote, category, posted_at, last_seen_at) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("_at"), as.Date),
                days_open = as.numeric(last_seen_at - posted_at))

# For Q1, to answer it, you need the following:
# - number of jobs
# - fraction of those jobs that are remote friendly


jobs |> 
  dplyr::group_by(category) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    postings = dplyr::n(), #counting the number of rows per category
    remote_share = mean(remote) |> round(3)
  )

#  Q2 Among the fulltime jobs, which states have the highest remote share?
jobs |> 
  dplyr::filter(category== 'fulltime') |> 
  dplyr::group_by(location_state) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    postings = dplyr::n(), #counting the number of rows per category
    remote_share = mean(remote) |> round(3)
) |> 
  dplyr::filter(postings >= 50) |> #up to you to determine the min threshold
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(remote_share))


jobs |> 
  dplyr::group_by(title) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    postings = dplyr::n(), #counting the number of rows per category
    remote_share = mean(remote) |> round(3),
    median_days_open = median(days_open))
  
by_state |> dplyr::left_join(states, by = "location_state")    # keep every row on the left
by_state |> dplyr::inner_join(states, by = "location_state")   # keep only the matches
by_state |> dplyr::anti_join(states, by = "location_state")    # keep only the non-matches

con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/midwest_airbnb.db")
listings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "listings") |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
dplyr::glimpse(listings)

listings |> 
  dplyr::group_by(city)
```
```{r}
states = tibble::tibble(location_state = state.abb,
                        state_name = state.name,
                        region = as.character(state.region))

jobs |>
  dplyr::left_join(states, by = "location_state") |>
  dplyr::group_by(region) |>
  dplyr::summarize(postings = dplyr::n(), remote_share = mean(remote)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(postings))

jobs |> dplyr::count(location_state) |> dplyr::anti_join(states, by = "location_state")
```

```{r}
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "../data/midwest_airbnb.db")
listings = DBI::dbReadTable(con, "listings") |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
dplyr::glimpse(listings)

#Q1: Approach A would be to count the repetitions within the city column
table(listings$city)

#alternatively, group by > summarize (n()) -- that returns a df in a we returned a named vector

listings |>
  dplyr::group_by(city) |>
  dplyr:: summarise(
    city_count = dplyr::n()
  ) -> practice_q1
practice_q1

#Q2: For entire homes (room_type == "Entire home/apt") that sleep four or more, what is the median price in each city?

listings |> 
  dplyr::filter(
    room_type == "Entire home/apt" & accommodates >= 4
    ) |> 
  dplyr:: group_by(city) |> 
  dplyr:: summarise(
    median_price = median(price)
  )

#Q3 Add price_per_person = price / accommodates. Which three listings are cheapest per person? Believe them?
#note that this is per listing, and we need to create a new column

listings |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    price_per_person = price/accommodates # LHS = new col name; RHS is the math used to create the new row by row]
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(price_per_person) |> 
  #next step is not neccessary
  dplyr::select(city, name, price, accommodates, price_per_person) |> 
  head(3) #tail would provide bottom 3 or most expensive since we are sorting in ascending order

#Q4 Which five host_names have the most listings?
listings |> 
  dplyr::count(host_name, host_id, sort = T)
```
